class.name: RopeBody3D
class.brief_description: A physically simulated rope or cable.
class.description: A chain of point masses joined by distance constraints, colliding along its whole length and able to be pinned or tied to a rigid body at any point along it. Unlike most physics nodes this inherits [MeshInstance3D] rather than [CollisionObject3D], because it produces deforming geometry rather than a rigid transform. The rope draws itself, and material slots, LOD and shadow settings come along for free. To set one up, give it a [member length], pick how many particles resolve it with [member point_count], and pin it: [member attach_start] and [member attach_end] cover the usual two-ended case, and the [member pin_count] array or [RopeAttachment3D] child nodes cover everything else. Length is independent of resolution, so adding points makes the rope smoother rather than longer. [b]Note:[/b] Ropes are implemented only by the Jolt Physics backend. On any other physics backend the node is inert and says so with a configuration warning in the editor. [b]Note:[/b] The simulation runs in world space while the mesh is generated in the node's local space. Moving the node at runtime therefore does not move a rope that is already simulating; call [method reset] for that. [b]Note:[/b] A rope is not a physics-server object, so no [Area3D] will ever report it in [method Area3D.get_overlapping_bodies]. Use [method get_ropes_in_area], [method is_in_area] or [method get_ratios_in_area] to ask the question from the rope's side instead.

method.name: apply_central_impulse
method.description: Applies [param impulse] to the rope as a whole, divided evenly among its particles, so the rope is pushed without being deformed.

method.name: apply_point_impulse
method.description: Applies [param impulse] to the single particle at [param point_index]. Use this to flick, snag or shoot a rope.

method.name: attach_point
method.description: Ties the particle at [param point_index] to [param body], keeping their current relative position. If [param body] is a dynamic [PhysicsBody3D] the two pull on each other; anything else acts as a pin the rope follows. This is the runtime equivalent of a pin in the [member pin_count] array. Use [method get_closest_ratio] to work out where along the rope to attach.

method.name: detach_point
method.description: Releases whatever the particle at [param point_index] was attached or pinned to, letting it swing free.

method.name: find_pin_at_index
method.description: Returns the index into the pin array of the pin that lands on the particle [param point_index], or [code]-1[/code] if no pin does.

method.name: get_closest_point
method.description: Returns the point on the rope nearest to [param world_point], in global coordinates. Unlike [method get_closest_ratio] this is measured along the segments rather than snapped to a particle, so it is the right thing to draw a marker at.

method.name: get_closest_ratio
method.description: Returns where along the rope [param world_point] is nearest, as a ratio from [code]0.0[/code] at the start to [code]1.0[/code] at the end. This is measured the same way pins and [RopeAttachment3D] measure it, so the result can be handed straight to one. This is how you grab a rope: take the hand or raycast position, ask for the ratio, and attach there.

method.name: get_collision_layer_value
method.description: Returns whether the layer [param layer_number] is set in [member collision_layer]. [param layer_number] is between 1 and 32.

method.name: get_collision_mask_value
method.description: Returns whether the layer [param layer_number] is set in [member collision_mask]. [param layer_number] is between 1 and 32.

method.name: get_physics_rid
method.description: Returns the [RID] of the underlying rope in [PhysicsServer3D], for direct server calls.

method.name: get_pin_node
method.description: Returns the node the pin at [param pin_index] is tied to, or an empty path if it pins the rope in place.

method.name: get_pin_offset
method.description: Returns the offset of the pin at [param pin_index] from its node, in that node's local space.

method.name: get_pin_ratio
method.description: Returns where along the rope the pin at [param pin_index] sits, from [code]0.0[/code] at the start to [code]1.0[/code] at the end.

method.name: get_point_position
method.description: Returns the global position of the particle at [param point_index].

method.name: get_point_velocity
method.description: Returns the velocity of the particle at [param point_index], in metres per second.

method.name: get_points
method.description: Returns the global positions of every particle, in order from start to end. This is the whole rope in one call and is much cheaper than looping over [method get_point_position].

method.name: get_ratios_in_area
method.description: Returns where this rope is inside [param area], as one ratio per particle that tests inside, ordered from start to end. Empty when the rope is clear of the area. Use this to tell [i]which part[/i] of a rope is affected — the submerged part, the part in the fire, the part inside a trigger volume. See [method is_in_area] when only a yes or no is needed. [b]Note:[/b] Particles are point-tested, so an area thinner than the spacing between particles can be missed. Raise [member point_count] if that matters.

method.name: get_ropes_in_area
method.description: Returns every [RopeBody3D] in the same world with at least one particle inside [param area]. Ropes are not physics-server objects and so are invisible to area monitoring — [method Area3D.get_overlapping_bodies] will never list one. This asks the question from the rope's side instead and needs no changes to the area at all. [b]Note:[/b] This is a query, not a monitor: it answers for the moment you call it and emits no signals. It costs a point query per particle per rope, so it suits being called on demand or on a timer rather than every frame for every rope in a level.

method.name: get_segment_length
method.description: Returns the rest length of a single segment, which is [member length] divided by one less than [member point_count].

method.name: get_simulated_length
method.description: Returns the rope's actual current length, summed along its segments. Compare against [member length] to see how much the rope is being stretched; with [member inextensible] on the two should stay equal.

method.name: is_in_area
method.description: Returns [code]true[/code] if any part of this rope is inside [param area]. Stops at the first particle that is, so it is cheaper than [method get_ratios_in_area] when the detail is not needed. See [method get_ropes_in_area] for why an [Area3D] cannot answer this itself.

method.name: is_point_pinned
method.description: Returns [code]true[/code] if the particle at [param point_index] is held by a pin or an attachment.

method.name: pin_point
method.description: Pins the particle at [param point_index] in place at its current position, or releases it if [param pin] is [code]false[/code]. A pinned particle is immovable and is what the rest of the rope hangs from.

method.name: reset
method.description: Returns the rope to its spawn pose and clears all motion. Because the simulation runs in world space, this is also how you move a rope that is already simulating: move the node, then call this.

method.name: sample_ratio
method.description: Returns the global position at [param ratio] along the rope, from [code]0.0[/code] at the start to [code]1.0[/code] at the end, interpolated between particles. Pairs with [method get_closest_ratio]: ask where something is on the rope, then track that spot as the rope moves.

method.name: set_collision_layer_value
method.description: Sets whether the layer [param layer_number] is set in [member collision_layer]. [param layer_number] is between 1 and 32.

method.name: set_collision_mask_value
method.description: Sets whether the layer [param layer_number] is set in [member collision_mask]. [param layer_number] is between 1 and 32.

method.name: set_pin_node
method.description: Ties the pin at [param pin_index] to the node at [param path]. A [PhysicsBody3D] becomes a real attachment; any other [Node3D] is a pin the rope follows; an empty path pins the rope in place.

method.name: set_pin_offset
method.description: Sets the offset of the pin at [param pin_index] from its node, in that node's local space. This is where on the body the rope is actually knotted.

method.name: set_pin_position
method.description: Moves the pin holding the particle at [param point_index] to [param position], in global coordinates. Only meaningful for a particle pinned in place; use this to drag a rope end around from a script.

method.name: set_pin_ratio
method.description: Sets where along the rope the pin at [param pin_index] sits, from [code]0.0[/code] at the start to [code]1.0[/code] at the end.

method.name: toggle_pin_at_ratio
method.description: Adds a pin at [param ratio] if there is not one there already, or removes the one that is. Returns the resulting pin count. This is what clicking a rope particle in the viewport does.

members.member: The node the far end of the rope (ratio [code]1.0[/code]) is tied to. A [PhysicsBody3D] here becomes a real attachment: the rope hangs from the body, and if the body is dynamic the two pull on each other. Any other [Node3D] acts as a pin the rope simply follows. This is exactly a pin at ratio [code]1.0[/code], and it is also one of the two points [constant LENGTH_FROM_ENDPOINTS] measures between.
The node the near end of the rope (ratio [code]0.0[/code]) is tied to. See [member attach_end], which behaves identically at the other end.

If [code]true[/code], a rope whose [member length] exceeds the straight distance between its outermost pins spawns already bowed downward by the excess, instead of spawning taut and visibly dropping on the first frame. This only shapes the starting pose. It has no effect once the rope is simulating.

How readily the rope curves. This is an inverse stiffness in metres per newton: [code]0.0[/code] is as stiff as the solver can make it, and larger values are floppier. At or above [code]1e6[/code] — the default — bending is switched off entirely and the rope is perfectly limp. Guide values, measured on a 2 m rope of 21 points at the default [member total_mass] and [member simulation_substeps]: - [code]1e6[/code] (default) — string, chain, cord. No resistance to curving whatsoever. - [code]1e-2[/code] — rubber tubing. Just barely holds a shape. - [code]1e-3[/code] — garden hose, thick electrical cable. - [code]1e-4[/code] — heavy-gauge cable. - [code]1e-5[/code] to [code]0.0[/code] — thick copper wire. Settles into the widest arc the rope's length allows and refuses to fold tightly. [b]Note:[/b] This resists [i]curvature[/i], not orientation. A straight rope hanging from a single pin has no curvature anywhere along it, so no amount of stiffness will hold it out horizontally the way a wire clamped in a vise would. What the setting governs is how tightly the rope is willing to fold. [b]Note:[/b] The effective stiffness also rises with [member simulation_substeps] and falls as [member total_mass] rises, so a large change to either is worth re-tuning this against.

If [code]true[/code], the rope collides with the world. Each segment is tested as a capsule, so the rope collides along its whole length rather than only at its particles. Turning this off is by far the cheapest way to make a rope faster, and is usually the right choice for purely decorative ones.
The physics layers this rope is on. Ropes are not queryable physics objects, so this exists for symmetry and for other ropes rather than for general queries.
The physics layers this rope scans for collisions. A collider is only considered if its own layer is in this mask.

Quadratic air drag. The rope is slowed in proportion to the [i]square[/i] of its speed, so this damps whipping and fast swinging far more than it damps slow settling — which is what makes a rope look like it is moving through air rather than through treacle. Set to [code]0.0[/code] to disable. See also [member linear_damping], which damps all motion equally.

Friction between the rope and whatever it touches, combined multiplicatively with the collider's own friction. [code]0.0[/code] slides freely; [code]1.0[/code] grips. This is what keeps a rope draped over a beam from sliding off it, and what carries a rope along on a moving platform.

Multiplier on the gravity the rope experiences. [code]0.0[/code] makes it weightless and negative values make it fall upward. Gravity is sampled per particle from the [Area3D]s the rope is in, so point gravity and custom gravity areas work as they do for rigid bodies.

If [code]true[/code], a hard limit is enforced on how long each segment may be, so the rope's total length can never exceed [member length] no matter what is pulling on it. This is what actually makes a rope behave like a rope rather than an elastic, and it should normally be left on. With it on, [member stretch_compliance] can only make the rope softer [i]within[/i] its length — it can never make the rope longer.
The direction the rope is laid out in when it spawns, used when [member spawn_curve] has not been shaped and the rope does not have two pins to span between.

The rope's total length along its own curve, in metres. This is a genuine input, not a result: it is independent of [member point_count], so changing the resolution makes the rope smoother or coarser without making it longer or shorter. Ignored unless [member length_mode] is [constant LENGTH_MANUAL], where it is used directly; the other modes compute it and write it here.
Where the rope's [member length] comes from. See [enum LengthMode].

Velocity damping applied to every particle, per second, independent of how fast the rope is moving. Use this to settle a rope down generally. For motion that should look like it is being resisted by air — whipping, fast swings — [member drag] is the more natural control, because it acts much more strongly on fast motion than on slow.

A ceiling on how hard the rope may [i]push[/i] an attached or contacted rigid body back into a position the rope allows, expressed as an impulse so it becomes a smaller speed change on a heavier body. This deliberately does [i]not[/i] limit the rope's ability to [i]stop[/i] a body. Stopping a body only removes energy and is what makes a rope come taut and hold; it is the push afterwards that can misbehave. Raise this if a heavy load takes too long to settle after a hard catch, lower it if light objects resting against a rope get nudged around too eagerly, and set it to [code]0.0[/code] to remove the limit entirely. Only relevant when [member two_way_coupling] is enabled or the rope is attached to a dynamic body.

The number of entries in the rope's pin array. Each pin holds one point of the rope, identified by a ratio from [code]0.0[/code] at the start to [code]1.0[/code] at the end, either in place or to a node. Pins are stored as ratios rather than particle indices, so they stay where you put them when [member point_count] changes. You can also add and remove them by clicking the rope's particles in the viewport.

The node this pin ties the rope to. A [PhysicsBody3D] becomes a real attachment that carries force; any other [Node3D] is a moving pin the rope follows. Leave empty to pin the rope in place at its spawn position.
Where on the pin's node the rope is knotted, in that node's local space.
Where along the rope this pin holds it, from [code]0.0[/code] at the start to [code]1.0[/code] at the end. Stored as a ratio so the pin stays put when [member point_count] changes.

How many particles the rope is resolved with. This is a quality and cost setting only — it does not change [member length]. More points means a smoother curve, tighter collision against small geometry, and finer control over where pins can sit, at a roughly linear cost.
How many sides the generated tube has. Only used when [member render_mode] is [constant RENDER_TUBE].
The rope's physical radius in metres. Used both for collision — each segment is a capsule of this radius — and for the thickness of the generated mesh, so the rope collides at the size it looks.
How the rope generates its mesh, or whether it generates one at all. See [enum RenderMode].
How much the rope bounces off what it hits, combined multiplicatively with the collider's own restitution. Real rope barely bounces at all, which is why this defaults to [code]0.0[/code].

How many solver substeps the rope takes per physics frame. Following the small-steps approach, the rope takes many substeps with one constraint iteration each rather than one step with many iterations, which converges far better for the same cost. More substeps means a stiffer, more accurate and more expensive rope. [b]Note:[/b] Effective stiffness scales with this, so changing it changes how [member stretch_compliance] and [member bend_compliance] behave.

Extra length given to the rope beyond the straight-line distance between its two attachment points, in metres. [code]0.0[/code] gives a rope pulled exactly taut, and larger values let it hang. Only used when [member length_mode] is [constant LENGTH_FROM_ENDPOINTS].

The shape the rope is in at the moment it spawns, in the node's local space. Drag the handles in the viewport to bend it. [b]Note:[/b] This is a starting pose, [i]not[/i] a rest shape. The rope does not spring back toward this curve and has no memory of it once the simulation starts — it exists so a rope can begin already bent, instead of spawning as a straight line through whatever happens to be in the way. To make a rope that resists being bent, use [member bend_compliance].

Inverse stiffness of the rope's length constraint, in metres per newton. [code]0.0[/code] is as rigid as the solver allows and larger values are stretchier. With [member inextensible] left on — the default — this only softens how the rope behaves within its length; it can never let the rope get longer. Turn [member inextensible] off to get a genuinely elastic rope. Measured that way, a 4 m rope at default mass carrying a 10 kg load settles at roughly: - [code]0.0[/code] to [code]1e-5[/code] — about 21% long. This floor is the solver's own softness at a 10:1 mass ratio rather than the compliance, so values in this range are all much the same. - [code]1e-4[/code] — about 27% long. A stiff synthetic rope with a little give. - [code]1e-3[/code] — about 89% long. Clearly elastic. - [code]1e-2[/code] — several times its own length. A bungee. For a rope that should not stretch, leave [member inextensible] on and ignore this setting.

The mass of the whole rope in kilograms, divided evenly among its particles. What matters is mostly the ratio between this and the mass of anything the rope is tied to or pushing against: a rope far lighter than its load will be dragged around by it, and a rope far heavier will barely notice.

If [code]true[/code], dynamic rigid bodies the rope touches are pushed back by it, so a rope can drag a crate along or hold one up. If [code]false[/code], the rope reacts to bodies but never pushes them, which is cheaper and cannot destabilise anything. [b]Note:[/b] A rope [i]attached[/i] to a dynamic body always transmits force to it regardless of this setting; this governs [i]contacts[/i]. Hard-pinning a rope end to a dynamic body would let the body drag that end wherever it went and force the rope to stretch without limit.

constants.constant: No mesh is generated. Use this when the rope is invisible, or when you draw it yourself from [method get_points].
The rope is drawn as a closed tube with [member radial_segments] sides. The better-looking option, and the right one for thick ropes seen close up.
The rope is drawn as a two-vertex-wide strip that turns to face the camera. Far cheaper than a tube and effectively indistinguishable for thin ropes, cables and wires.
[member length] is used exactly as set.
[member length] is the straight-line distance between the two attachment points plus [member slack], recomputed as they move apart. This is the mode to use for a rope strung between two things.
[member length] is the arc length of [member spawn_curve], so the rope is exactly as long as the shape drawn in the viewport.
